title: The 10x Programmer Myth
summary: Argues the 10x programmer is a myth assembled from archetypes whose hidden costs fall on teammates, and that avoiding net-negative developers matters more than hunting stars.

assertions.quote: Compared to someone like this, everyone is a 10x programmer!

verdicts.note: Re-analyses of the classic studies show best-to-worst ratios of ten or more but quartile ratios nearer two to four, so the gap depends on which tail you include.

The large max/min ratios in the Grant/Sackman groups usually stem from a single very slow subject, so extreme measured gaps are driven by slow outliers rather than exceptional fast ones; the report does not characterise those outliers as net-negative.

assertions.quote: really all they are doing is leaning on the rest of the team to make themselves look productive
If you can reduce distractions, focus, and get into flow, then you’ll automatically be more effective than most software engineers.
By avoiding a lot of extra software and overly complex processes, these developers can save their teams countless hours.
Once they reach a solution, you can be sure that people aren’t going to have to come behind them and clean things up.

verdicts.note: Upfront understanding reduces rework in design studies, though the optimal amount varies and this is an archetype, not data.

assertions.quote: If John Carmack was dropped into the average web development project, he wouldn’t be very happy or effective

verdicts.note: Expertise is domain-specific per expertise research, though top engineers often transfer reasonably well.

Changes from developers with little prior activity on a Windows component predict failures, and the same developers are usually major contributors to a dependent component, i.e. expertise is component-specific; the outcome measured is defects, not productivity.
